Diseases of RBC & Bleeding Disorders IPathology LEC · LE #3 · Dr. Araceli P. Jacoba · 10/24/2025

Lesson Overview

The lecture builds from normal hematopoiesis to anemia, then to hemolytic anemia and the specific hemolytic disorders.

  • Anemia: reduction of the total circulating red cell mass to below normal limits resulting in DEC oxygen transport.
  • Anemia is diagnosed by laboratory tests (Hb, Hct, reticulocyte count, PBS, RBC indices), classified by morphology, then traced to a cause.
  • Hemolytic anemia is sorted into intravascular vs extravascular hemolysis before naming the disorder.

Most Important Must-Know Concepts

Must Know
  • MCV and MCHC are best used in determining RBC morphology.
  • Non-functioning marrow: DEC reticulocyte count in anemia indicates bone marrow failure.
  • EJK: Erythroid hyperplasia, Jaundice, Chromatosis/Color.
  • Methemoglobinemia and DEC serum haptoglobin are intravascular findings
    • Jaundice, anemia are common to both
  • Majority of hemolysis from an intrinsic red cell defect occurs in the spleen (extravascular)
    • Splenomegaly does not occur in IVH
  • INC in reticulocytes is expected in hemolytic anemia.
  • G6PD: two types of hemolysis present
    • Sickle cell: vaso-occlusive crisis
    • Thalassemia: β and α subtypes and the hypochromic microcytic anemia table

Learning Objectives

  • To understand the different types of anemia, its causes, symptomatology, laboratory diagnosis based on RBC alterations and prognosis
  • To understand hemolysis
  • To understand bleeding disorder

A. Site of Hematopoiesis p. 1

SiteKey points
Yolk sac
  • First organ responsible for the production of blood in the fetus
  • Starts as early as 4 weeks or 1st month of embryogenesis until the 3rd month, after which the spleen takes over
SpleenTook over at the 3rd month
Liver
  • Main hematopoietic organ in the fetus
  • From 4 weeks until the child is born
  • Produces majority of the blood requirements of the fetus
Bone marrowTakes over as the main hematopoietic organ at birth

Bone marrow through life

  • Liver is no longer active unless there is anemia in the developing fetus, like in hydrops fetalis, causing extramedullary hematopoiesis
  • When a child is born: all the bones are active
    • As one grows older, the long bones contribute lesser and lesser to hematopoiesis
  • At 18 years old: only the central bones (vertebrae, pelvis, sternum, and ribs) are hematologically active
  • At about 40 to 50 years old: minimal or no contribution from femur or long bones
    • 50% of the marrow remains active in the adults
  • Bone marrow aspirates are obtained from the pelvic bone
    • It has the most hematopoietic activity throughout a patient's lifetime
Pathologic conditions
  • Long bones and skull can develop hematopoietic activity in anemia
  • The more bones recruited for hematopoiesis, the more severe the anemia is

B. Hemoglobin Structure p. 1–2

  • Hemoglobin structure varies during development
  • Fetus: the red cell contains HbF (alpha-2, gamma-2 globin chain)
    • Main hemoglobin at birth and decreases until 6 months of age
    • Some hematologic diseases start to manifest symptoms only at 6 months, when HbF is no longer present in the blood
  • Adult hemoglobin
    • 95% HbA (α2β2)
    • 3–5% HbA2 (α2δ2)
  • HbA1C is a subtype of HbA increased in diabetic patients
    • Used to monitor sugar levels
    • Not involved in hematologic disorders
  • Hemoglobin containing Epsilon and Zeta are very immature forms produced in the yolk sac
    • Once the liver takes over hematopoiesis, these are lost in the system

C. Normal Hematopoiesis p. 2

  • Starts with the hematopoietic stem cell (HSC), a pluripotent or multipotent cell capable of self renewal
  • HSC differentiates further into separate stem cells or progenitor cells
Hematopoietic Stem Cell (HSC)

Myeloid Stem Cell

  • Source of red cells, platelets, neutrophils, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils
  • Red cells and platelets originate from the same stem cell that produces granulocytes and monocytes
  • Some diseases of red cells will have problems with platelets and granulocytic WBC when the myeloid stem cell is involved

Lymphoid Stem Cell

  • Produces B and T lymphocytes

Beyond the blood vessels

Below the horizontal orange line in Figure 3 = intravascular space

  • Monocyte → macrophages
  • Basophil → mast cells
  • B-lymphocytes → plasma cells
Table 1. Stimulatory controls to hematopoiesis
CellsStimulatory control
Pluripotent stem cells (production of more myelocytes)Stem Cell Factor (SCF) and IL-6
Myeloid stem cellsSCF, IL-3 and IL-6
Erythrocyte productionErythropoietin (EPO)
Platelet productionThrombopoietin (TPO)

D. Red Cell Maturation p. 2

Maturity involves

  • DEC in cell size
  • Condensation of the chromatin (pyknotic) and loss of nucleus
  • Change in the color of cytoplasm from blue to red as it takes more hemoglobin

The whole process from stimulus by the EPO until the last stage of development takes 3 to 5 days.

Pronormoblast · largest and most immature cell: large nucleus, present nucleoli, and blue cytoplasm
Basophilic normoblast · dark blue cytoplasm, denser chromatin, nucleoli present
Polychromatic normoblast · polychromatophilic cytoplasm (mixture of red and blue), smaller nucleus without nucleoli
Orthochromatic normoblast · orange/reddish cytoplasm with very dense ink blot nuclei
Polychromatophilic erythrocyte / Reticulocyte · no nuclei · first cell present in the peripheral blood
Mature red cell / Erythrocyte

Definition p. 3

Core definition
  • Anemia: Reduction of the total circulating red cell mass to below normal limits resulting in DEC oxygen transport
  • Not concerned with any other component of blood
  • Only concerned with the number or volume of red cells and its hemoglobin content

A. Signs and Symptoms

  • Nonspecific
  • Weakness, malaise, easy fatigability, dyspnea on mild exertion, headache, dizziness
    • Represent decrease in oxygenation to the tissues
  • Same manifestations are also present in diseases of the heart, lungs, patients with malignancies, and even prodrome of an infection

B. Physical Exam

FindingKey points
Pallor Must KnowMost consistent finding of anemia
  • Examining skin is subjective due to skin tone variations
  • Best area to evaluate: conjunctiva, floor of the mouth, and palms of the hands
MurmursCalled "hemic murmur"
  • Characterized by systolic, low grade murmur (1 or 2 over 5)
    • 5 = loudest murmur grade
    • If not systolic nor low grade, it might be a pathologic cardiac murmur
  • Due to the decreasing viscosity of the blood, creating turbulence in the cardiac chambers during systole
AnginaMay be present when the decreased oxygenation compromises the heart supply in an occluded coronary vessel
Oliguria (DEC urine volume) & anuria (no urine)
  • Present only if anemia is due to blood loss
  • Hemoglobinopathy or nutritional anemia will not cause oliguria
Brittle nails or koilonychia (spooning of the nails)
  • Present in chronic anemia or long standing condition
  • Prolonged oxygen deprivation to the nail beds
  • Not specific for anemia
  • Seen in chronic lung diseases
Exam trap Murmurs, oliguria, and koilonychia are not always present in patients with anemia but are seen in other conditions.

C. Laboratory Diagnosis p. 3

  • Symptoms and PE of anemia are nonspecific
  • A laboratory test is required for diagnosis

Hemoglobin and Hematocrit

  • Anemia is based on the levels of hemoglobin and hematocrit
    • Values below normal are considered anemic
  • Higher normal values in males because of the monthly losses in females
  • Normal values vary according to location and race
    • Caucasians have higher hemoglobin levels than Asians
    • People living in highlands have higher hemoglobin content than people living in lowlands

Reticulocyte count (NV: 0.5–1.5%)

  • Determines bone marrow activity
  • In anemia, elevated reticulocyte count is expected
    • It is a physiologic response to red cell loss (functioning bone marrow)
Must Know Non-functioning marrow: DEC reticulocyte count in anemia indicates bone marrow failure.

Peripheral smear (PBS)

  • Determines morphology

RBC distribution width (11.5–14.5)

  • Determines anisocytosis (variability in size) and poikilocytosis (variability in shape)
  • INC RDW = more variability in red cell size and shape
Table 2. Normal values
FemaleMale
Hb12–14 g/dL13–16 g/dL
Hct33–42%39–48%
Retic count0.5–1.5%
PBSNormochromic, normocytic
RDW11.5–14.5

E. Peripheral Blood Smear p. 4

Can also provide the morphology of the red blood cell.

Size: compare the red cell with the smallest lymphocyteColor: central pallor of the red cell
Normocytic: same size or only slightly smaller than the smallest lymphocyteNormochromic: ⅓ the diameter of the red blood cell
Microcytic: significantly smaller than the smallest lymphocyteHypochromic: greater than ⅓
Macrocytic: larger than smallest lymphocyteHyperchromic: small or almost lost

G. Causes of Anemia p. 4–5

Causes of anemia

Blood loss

  • Lose blood from intravascular space
  • Can be acute or chronic

Hemolysis

Increased rate of destruction

Impaired red cell production

Deficiency in any requirement of erythrogenesis

Blood loss
Acute blood lossChronic blood loss
  • Normochromic, normocytic
  • Loss of large amount of blood in a short period of time (ex: vehicular accidents with gaping injury)
  • Lose 1000cc within 10–15 mins
  • Manifestation: cardiovascular collapse with hypotension and shock
  • Hypochromic, microcytic
  • Due to undetected or occult bleeding → losses of iron which is not replaced
  • In elderly → check for malignancy

Acute blood loss: physiological changes in blood after survival

  • Shift of interstitial fluid to the intravascular space, aggravating the decreased red cell and anemia
  • DEC BP → mobilizes the granulocytes in the BM, the first response in injury
  • First manifestation: leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, reticulocytosis (occurs after 3–5 days)
  • DEC O2 → trigger EPO release
    • EPO induces reticulocytosis, but this occurs 3–5 days after the injury
    • Leukocytosis and thrombocytosis occur immediately

Hemolysis (increased rate of destruction)

  • BM compensates when the life span of RBC is shortened (<120 days)
    • INC BM activity is expected in all cases of hemolysis
Intrinsic causes: hereditary, internal to the red cellExtrinsic causes: outside the red cell
  • G6PD
  • Sickle cell
  • PK deficiency
  • Spherocytosis
  • Thalassemia
  • Malaria
  • Antibody-mediated
  • Lead poisoning
  • SLE

Impaired red cell production

  • BM has to continuously replace the red cell, which has a life span of 120 days
    • Without replacement → expect anemia
DefectExamples
Defective DNA synthesisB12 & folic acid deficiency
Defective Hb synthesis
  • Iron deficiency (heme)
  • Thalassemia (globin)
Disturbance of proliferation of stem cell
  • Aplastic anemia
  • Anemia in renal failure

A. General Characteristics p. 5

Must Know · EJK Erythroid hyperplasia · Jaundice · Chromatosis/Color
  • Premature destruction of RBC
  • INC erythropoiesis
    • Erythroid hyperplasia
      • INC normoblasts: start to appear in the peripheral blood
        • Normally reside in the BM and are never seen in blood unless the patient has anemia
      • INC reticulocyte count
      • INC cellularity in the BM: E:M (erythroid:myeloid) ratio 1:1 (normal E:M ratio 1:4–5)
    • Extramedullary hematopoiesis: hematopoiesis active outside the BM
      • Ex: liver (in young patients), skull and long bones (in older patients)
      • These organs do not contribute much but are recruited when the body needs more blood
  • Accumulation of the products of hemoglobin catabolism
    • Jaundice: predominantly unconjugated bilirubin (B1)
      • Increased B1 → pigment stones in the gallbladder
    • Hemochromatosis: INC Hb catabolism = INC iron accumulation
      • INC hemosiderin → brown color
      • INC iron storage in siderocytes/blast
  • INC Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)
    • Abundant enzyme in red cells
      • Elevates in serum once red cells lyse

Intravascular vs Extravascular p. 5

Lecturer emphasis
  • After determining that the anemia is hemolytic, you need to know if the hemolysis occurs intravascularly or extravascularly
  • Methemoglobin, hemoglobinuria and decreasing haptoglobin can only be seen in intravascular hemolysis
  • Jaundice, increasing iron stores, and hemosiderin are present in both

B. Intravascular Hemolysis p. 5–6

Events upon death or lysis of the RBC within the blood vessel

Hb released into blood
Hb attaches to haptoglobin for transport to the RES
Final degradation in the spleen
Haptoglobin decreases from circulation
More free Hb in blood (hemoglobinemia) or urine (hemoglobinuria)
Change in red/brown color of urine
Clinical cue
  • A change in the color of the urine and decreasing haptoglobin levels are both important indicators of intravascular lysis
  • Example: a patient with malaria would have a primary complaint of change in urine color since the parasite causes intravascular lysis of RBC
  • Oxidation of Hb to methemoglobin (methemoglobinemia) and combination with its transport protein (methaemalbuminaemia)
    • Oxidation of the hemoglobin's iron from ferrous (Fe2+) to ferric (Fe3+)
    • It is the ferric iron contained in methemoglobin
    • Ferric is nonfunctional: limited capacity to bind oxygen
  • Hemosiderin production as a byproduct of heme degradation
    • Brownish color when excreted in the urine (hemosiderinuria)

Characteristics of intravascular hemolysis

FindingKey points
1. Presence of free Hb
  • Release of Hb in blood (hemoglobinemia)
  • Excreted in the urine as hemoglobinuria
  • Lecturer You don't see hemoglobinuria if it is extravascular alone
2. Methemoglobinemia Must KnowFrom oxidation of hemoglobin to methemoglobin
3. DEC serum haptoglobin Must Know
  • Important laboratory parameter in the diagnosis of intravascular hemolysis
  • It binds to free Hb in blood and carries it to the spleen
4. Hemosiderinuria
  • Production of hemosiderin as a byproduct of heme degradation
  • Brownish color when excreted in the urine
Plus: jaundice, anemia Must KnowCommon to both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis

Causes of intravascular hemolysis

  • Majority of the hemoglobinopathies are extravascular in nature
  • Majority (of intravascular causes) are extrinsic defects to the red cell
  • Only few intrinsic red cell abnormalities cause intravascular hemolysis
CauseExamples
Mechanical injury
  • Heart valve defects
  • Trauma to red cells passing through obstructions: prosthetic heart valves, or microthrombi caused by DIC or TTP
Antibodies
  • Transfusion mismatch
  • Antibody destruction
InfectionsMalaria
Common causes of IVH
  • G6PD deficiency
  • Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)

C. Extravascular Hemolysis p. 6

  • Occurs in the spleen and liver
  • Spleen and reticuloendothelial system (RES) are the graveyard of senescent and defective RBCs
  • Spleen degrades Hb into its final end products: iron, hemosiderin, bilirubin
  • Spleen plays a major role in extravascular hemolysis
    • Splenomegaly is present only in extravascular, not in intravascular types of hemolysis
Must Know · Take note
  • Majority of hemolysis from an intrinsic red cell defect occurs in the spleen or is extravascular in nature
  • Having an intrinsic RBC defect means you have an abnormal or damaged RBC
  • The spleen views the abnormal RBC as a foreign material and eliminates it

Characteristics of extravascular hemolysis

  • Limited to RES, particularly the spleen
    • No elevation in free hemoglobin or hemoglobin breakdown products in the blood or urine (only observed in IVH)
  • Anemia
  • Jaundice
  • Splenomegaly Must Know
    • Does not occur in IVH since the spleen is the site of lysis for the defective RBCs

D. Histology p. 6

Normal E:M ratio / bone marrowErythroid hyperplasia
  • 1 erythroid precursor for every 4–5 myeloid precursors
  • Majority of cells in the marrow are stabs (last cell before entering the circulation)
  • WBCs are replaced with erythroid precursors (increased erythropoiesis)
  • Myeloid precursors < erythroid precursors
  • DEC number of stabs or none at all
  • Smear is overpowered by numerous normoblasts or RBC precursors

Reticulocytes p. 7

  • Young RBC that lost their nucleus
  • Nuclear fragments have disintegrated and cause a reticular appearance as seen on methylene blue stain
    • Represents disintegration of the nucleus of a normoblast forming a network of granular or reticular chromatid
Must Know INC in reticulocytes is expected in hemolytic anemia.
Methylene blue stain (supravital staining)Wright's stain
Reticular network of degenerating nucleus is visible
  • Appear as slightly larger polychromatophilic cells
  • Reticular network cannot be seen

IV. Hemolytic Disorders p. 7

Hemolytic anemia: INC destruction of the red cell in peripheral blood causing a DEC in the survival of red cells (<120 days life span).

List: Spherocytosis · G6PD · Sickle cell anemia · Thalassemia · PNH · AHA · Microangiopathic

A. Hereditary Spherocytosis

Definition Congenital defect of the surface proteins (spectrin, actin, ankyrin) in red cells which normally maintain the biconcave shape of RBC.
  • Biconcave shape helps the RBC become more durable and deformable as it passes through capillaries or splenic sinusoids with smaller diameter
  • The central concavity corresponds to the central pallor of the RBC

Pathogenesis

Abnormality of membrane proteins spectrin, actin, ankyrin
Sphere instead of discoid shape
Inflexible when passing small capillaries, esp. spleen
Hemolysis
  • PBS: RBC is spheroidal (similar to marbles), loss of central pallor
    • Spherocytes are distinctive but pathognomonic
    • Can be an acquired shape in autoimmune hemolytic anemia and hemolytic disease of the newborn
  • Symptoms are secondary to extravascular hemolysis from rupture of RBCs in the splenic sinusoids
    • Main manifestations: anemia, splenomegaly, and jaundice

Study note: because spherocytes can also be acquired (AIHA, hemolytic disease of the newborn), the shape alone does not name HS.

Membrane defect → spherocyte (Figure 14)

  • Left of Figure 14: the 3 structural proteins intertwine to support the cytoplasmic membrane
  • Abnormality causes weakness to the cell membrane → loss in cytosol
  • To compensate for the lost volume, red cells assume a more spherical shape
  • Spherocyte is much smaller, rounded, with no central pallor compared with the normal red cell
    • Red cell indices: MCHC (color) is INC and MCV (volume) is DEC
    • PBS: microcytic hyperchromic appearance

Splenic Trapping p. 8

Lecturer emphasis
  • Normal RBC size: 7.5 to 8 micron
  • From the sides: only 2.5 micron
  • This thin portion is necessary for the red cell to pass through the sinusoids of the spleen (it passes side view through the narrow passage)

In hereditary spherocytosis

  • No narrow portion in a spherocyte → red cell lyses while negotiating passage through the spleen
  • The RBC shape contributes to splenic trapping, causing sluggishness of blood flow
  • DEC passage time through the spleen aggravates hemolysis by:
    • Decreasing nutrients (glucose & ATP)
    • Increasing lactic acid causing acidosis
    • Allowing greater contact time with the macrophages
Lecturer emphasis
  • All these contribute to hemolysis
  • Splenomegaly is a major manifestation of this disorder
  • Surgical removal of the spleen will correct the anemia

Signs & Symptoms p. 8

  • Clinical picture depends on how well the bone marrow can compensate for hemolysis
  • Manifestation is due to the extravascular type of hemolysis
  • EJK + anemia, splenomegaly
  • Splenectomy corrects anemia
  • In all forms of hemolysis, the bone marrow response is necessary for survival
PresentationBasis
Asymptomatic (20–30%)Erythropoiesis is greater than hemolysis
Chronic hemolytic anemiaErythropoiesis is less than hemolysis = chronic hemolysis producing EJK
Course: stable, unless interrupted by critical episodes
CrisisDescriptionCause
Aplastic crisisAttacks the stem cells of the bone marrowParvovirus infection
Hemolytic crisisSudden lysis of all red cells passing through the spleen causing hypotensionInfectious mononucleosis

Laboratory Diagnosis: Osmotic Fragility Test p. 8

  • Laboratory test to diagnose spherocytosis
  • Series of saline test tubes with decreasing concentration of NSS (0.9 to 0.2 NSS)
  • Normal red cells lie at 0.45 to 0.5 NSS concentration
Hemolysis at higher concentrationHemolysis at lower concentration
  • Hereditary spherocytosis
  • A spherocyte is small and bulging or full
  • Lesser amount of water enters before rupture
  • Rupture occurs earlier, in higher concentrations
  • Sickle cells
  • More water enters before rupture
  • Rupture occurs on lower concentrations
  • The test is not done for sickle cell or disorders with lower-than-normal concentrations

B. Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) Deficiency p. 8

  • X-linked recessive condition: predominantly affects the male population
  • 2 variants
    • G6PD(-): only mature RBC lack the enzyme
    • G6PD Mediterranean: more serious
      • All RBC lack enzyme
Lecturer emphasis
  • Intravascular since there is hemoglobinuria, but still contains bite cells and Heinz bodies
  • Bite cells and Heinz bodies are degraded in the spleen (extravascular hemolysis)
  • Intravascular hemolysis is much more predominant in G6PD, caused by hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)

Pathogenesis p. 9

With G6PD (normal pathway)Without G6PD
  • Enzyme for reactions changing glucose → 6-phosphogluconate
  • Produces important antioxidants NADPH and reduced glutathione together with Hb+2
  • These prevent oxidative stress and protect red cells from lysis
  • Produces NADP, H2O2, and Hb+3
  • These oxidized substances cause damage to the cell through the production of ROS or free radicals
  • Glutathione, in its oxidized form, is metabolized to H2O2

NADP, glutathione

  • Responsible for the intravascular type of hemolysis

Methemoglobin with Fe3+

  • Denatured hemoglobin that becomes the Heinz bodies

Heinz bodies

  • Interpreted as foreign by the spleen → engulfed → produces the bite cells → extravascular hemolysis
  • Fe+2 or Hb+2 is the functional form that carries oxygen
    • Oxidized Fe+3 cannot carry oxygen
  • Usually seen as solitary inclusions at the margins of red cells
  • Heinz bodies can damage the membrane to cause intravascular hemolysis
Must Know Two types of hemolysis present (intravascular and extravascular).
  • PBS: normochromic, normocytic anemia, INC reticulocytes, Heinz bodies, bite cells
    • Bite cells form when the splenic macrophage plucks out the Heinz bodies, which may also cause the mild extravascular hemolysis
  • G6PD is needed to revert oxidative substances back to their functional form once exposed to oxidative stress

Precipitating Factors p. 9

Oxidant drugs, fava beans, infection, stress

  • Infections, chemicals, drugs, and stress all stimulate the oxidation and utilization of glucose → leads to O2-deprived free radicals
Lecturer emphasis
  • If you become symptomatic when you eat fava beans, you're most likely to have G6PD deficiency, a condition called favism
  • In an infection, you need a lot of NADPH oxidase (phagocyte oxidase) → produces ROS needed for killing

Signs & Symptoms p. 9

  • Episodic type of hemolysis: only becomes symptomatic upon exposure to an oxidative condition
  • Intravascular / extravascular hemolysis 2–3 days after exposure (anemia, change in color of urine)
    • Intravascular outweighs extravascular lysis
  • ROS, free radicals, Heinz bodies, elevated oxidized substances all contribute to intravascular hemolysis
  • Extravascular (spleen) lysis is due to Heinz bodies destroyed by the spleen
  • Mild extravascular hemolysis
  • No symptoms of chronic hemolysis

Typical presentation

Exposure to oxidative substance
Anemia 2–3 days after exposure + change in urine color (hemoglobinuria)
Self-limited, recovery in 5–7 days (↑ reticulocytes)
Destroyed red cells replaced → back to normal

The 5–7 day frame corresponds to the time from stimulation of normoblast to appearance of RBC in PBS.

C. Sickle Cell Anemia p. 9

Definition
  • Missense mutation causing the substitution of glutamine for valine in the 6th position of the beta chain
  • Producing HbS instead of HbA
  • HbS: α2β2 6Val

Pathogenesis p. 9–10

Deoxygenation
HbS aggregates and polymerizes
Distortion
Sickling of RBC

(1) Chronic hemolysis

In the spleen (extravascular)

(2) Small vessel occlusion → ischemia

Main manifestation of ischemic episodes: Pain

  • HbS causes distortion and polymerization of red cells → sickle cells or holly leaf appearance once oxygen is removed from hemoglobin
    • It is important to keep hemoglobin attached to oxygen to prevent sickling
  • Sickle cells form clumps which prevent blood flow → ischemia and infarction
    • Sickle cells express higher than normal levels of adhesion molecules and are sticky, causing clumping
  • Autosplenectomy: repeated cycle of infarction, repair, and fibrosis converts the whole spleen into a completely fibrotic organ
Table 5. Variants of sickle cell anemia
Sickle cell anemiaSickle cell trait
Genetic make-upHomozygousHeterozygous
% HbS90–100%20–40%, the rest HbA
SymptomPlugging of cap ⇒ pain and infarction in different organsNo sx. unless exposed to low O2
Spleen
  • Enlarged in infancy
  • Small adults: autosplenectomy
Normal
PBS
  • Normochromic, normocytic
  • (+) Sickle cells
  • (+) Normoblasts
Hb identificationSingle large band: HbS
  • Small band: HbS
  • Large band: HbA
Other lab abnormalitiesDEC osmotic fragility and ESRNone
PrognosisFatal at 20 y/oNormal life span

Diagnosis p. 10

  • Electrophoresis provides a definitive diagnosis based on identification of Hemoglobin S (HbS)
    • Can also identify the variant of sickle cell in the patient
  • Sickle cell trait (upper graph): two hemoglobin peaks, almost equal quantities of HbA and HbS
  • Sickle cell anemia (bottom graph): only one peak representing HbS
    • The usual HbA position is absent

Factors Affecting Sickling p. 10–11

Uncontrollable factors: amount of sickling depends on the type of Hb that coexists with HbS

InteractionEffect
HbS = HbS
  • Greatest amount of sickling
  • Greater sickling in sickle cell anemia with 100% HbS
HbS = HbA
  • Less sickling
  • Less sickling in sickle cell trait with <50% HbS
HbF ≠ HbS
  • Sickling does not occur if HbF is present
  • Symptoms are never present <6 months of age or when HbF persists in circulation
HbC (6lys) ⇉ polymerization of HbS
  • HbC + HbS = HbSC
  • Mild sickling
  • Easily lose water → INC concentration of Hb → sickling (milder than HbS)

Controllable factors: advise patient to avoid these to prevent triggering of sickling

FactorMechanism
INC MCHC and intracellular dehydration
  • DEC intravascular fluid → increase in MCHC → increased interaction between red cells and hemoglobin
  • Avoid dehydration in patient
DEC pH
  • Acidosis → DEC oxygen affinity
  • Removing oxygen from HbS is the trigger for sickling
INC transit time through vasculature
  • Promotes stasis → release of oxygen → sickling → vascular occlusion
  • Normal vasculature is short (no time for aggregation) except in spleen and bone marrow, where circulation has a long transit time and most sickling occurs
Inflammation (INC transit time, DEC pH)
  • Infection → leukocytes adhere to endothelium → transudation of fluid → stasis
  • Explains why sickle cell patients become symptomatic during an infection
Length of exposure to DEC oxygenMicrovasculature in bone marrow and spleen: greatest sickling

Signs and Symptoms p. 11

  • Capillary stasis and thrombosis
    • Vascular occlusion → infarction and stroke
    • Pulmonary compromise: pulmonary infections lead to sickling → potentially fatal cycle of worsening hypoxia, sickling, and vasoocclusion
    • Priapism and loss of visual acuity or blindness: DEC blood flow to the penis and eye from adhesion of sickle cells to the endothelium of narrow vessels
  • Splenomegaly at onset of disease and progression to autosplenectomy
  • Predisposition to infection of encapsulated organisms such as Pneumococcus and H. influenzae
    • Splenic clearance is impaired by capsule of organisms
    • In adults: impaired splenic function is due to autosplenectomy
    • In children: impaired splenic function is due to congestion and DEC blood flow

Laboratory Abnormalities p. 11

  • Evidences of chronic hemolysis: EJK
    • INC RBC destruction → anemia, formation of bilirubin, hemosiderin, and iron overload
  • INC erythropoiesis
    • Extramedullary hematopoiesis in the skull, facial bones and long bones due to severe anemia
    • Skull x-ray: "crew haircut" appearance, enlarged cheeks
    • Hyperplastic bone marrow with increased young red cells (reticulocytes and normoblasts) spilling into peripheral blood
  • PBS
    • Sickle cells: holly leaf (Christmas leaf) appearance
    • Howell-Jolly bodies: round solitary nuclear remnants in red cells due to asplenia

Critical Episodes p. 11

Must Know · Vaso-occlusive (pain) crisis Multiple, simultaneous painful thrombosis in different organs that can be triggered by any factors that promote sickling (e.g., acidosis, dehydration, infection).
CrisisKey points
Vaso-occlusive crisis Must KnowOrgans involved: bones (common in children), lungs, liver, spleen, brain, penis
  • Hand foot syndrome: multiple bones of hands and feet
    • Need to differentiate from osteomyelitis
  • Acute chest syndrome: multiple thrombosis in different areas of the lungs
    • Patient appears like they are having a heart attack
    • Fever, cough, chest pain, infection → sluggish flow → sickling and vaso-occlusion
Aplastic crisis
  • Sudden failure of bone marrow to increase RBC production despite anemia
  • Caused by Parvovirus infection that attacks hematopoietic stem cells
Sequestration crisis
  • Massive destruction of almost all RBC passing through the spleen → sudden acute splenic enlargement → hypovolemia → shock
  • Seen in children with functional, intact spleen

D. Thalassemia p. 11

  • Pathology: defective globin synthesis or absent globin chain
  • Clinical manifestations vary widely due to heterogeneity of mutations
  • Genetically heterogeneous disorder caused by germline mutations that decrease the synthesis of α-globin or β-globin → anemia, tissue hypoxia, and red cell hemolysis related to imbalance in globin chain synthesis

β-Thalassemia: absent or defective β-globin chain Must Know

Table 6. Subtypes of β-thalassemia
SubtypeAllelesCharacteristics
β-Thalassemia Minorβ+/β or β0/β
  • Asymptomatic with very mild anemia
  • Cooley's trait
β-Thalassemia Intermediaβ+/β0 or mild β+/β+
  • Intermediate between the minor and major
  • Symptomatic form of anemia which may occasionally require transfusion
β-Thalassemia Majorβ+/β+ or β0/β0
  • Severe form where transfusion is necessary for survival
  • Transfusion-dependent type
  • Cooley's anemia
Lecture-specific note Not required to memorize alleles for each syndrome, but need to know the clinical manifestations.

α-Thalassemia: absent or defective α-globin chain Must Know

  • Normal individuals have four α-globin genes
    • Severity depends on the number of deleted α-globin genes
  • β and γ chains in α-thalassemia are more soluble than the α-α combinations in β-thalassemia
    • Thus, hemolysis and ineffective erythropoiesis are less severe in α-thalassemia compared to β-thalassemia
Table 7. Subtypes of α-thalassemia
SubtypeCharacteristics
Mild forms
Silent carrier
  • Deletion of one α-globin gene (minimal and barely detectable)
  • No symptoms, no RBC abnormalities except very mild microcytosis
α-Thalassemia trait
  • Deletion of two α-globin genes, α-globin production decreased by 50%
  • Asymptomatic with mild anemia (like β-thalassemia minor)
Severe forms
Hemoglobin H (HbH) disease
  • Deletion of three α-globin genes
  • Only one functioning α-globin gene → severe decrease in α-globin → β-globin pairs with another β-globin → HbH = four β-globin chains (in adults)
  • Absent α-globin → high affinity to oxygen → severe tissue hypoxia
Hydrops fetalis (Barts Hb)
  • Deletion of four α-globin genes
  • Recall: HbF in the infant = two α-globin + two γ-globin
  • Complete absence of α-globin → γ-globin pairs with another γ-globin → four γ-globin chains (in infants)
  • Absent α-globin → high affinity to oxygen → severe tissue hypoxia

Pathogenesis of Anemia in Thalassemia p. 12

DEC rate of globin synthesis → abnormal Hb → hypochromic microcytic anemia
Aggregation and precipitation of unpaired globin → abnormal erythropoiesis: flawed red cells, young RBCs die early
RBCs with inclusions destroyed by the spleen (extravascular hemolysis contributes to anemia)
Severe anemia: bone marrow replaces destroyed RBCs with other defective RBCs
Only means of survival is transfusion → transfused RBCs have shorter life spans → severe hemosiderosis

Signs and Symptoms p. 12

  • Due to chronic severe hemolysis (EJK in its severe form)
  • Massive erythroid hyperplasia with expansion of red marrow
    • Skull x-ray: "crew haircut" appearance
    • Enlargement of the face/cheek with small jaw from involvement of the maxilla in extramedullary hematopoiesis
  • Hemosiderosis / Hemochromatosis: severe due to iron overload and non-excretion, depositing in skin, pancreas, heart and liver
    • Skin: brown discoloration
    • Pancreas: can cause diabetes
    • "Brown diabetics" from deposition in the skin and pancreas
    • Cardiac hemochromatosis can cause death in patients with frequent transfusions
  • Massive hepatosplenomegaly due to extramedullary hematopoiesis
  • Jaundice due to extravascular hemolysis
  • Normal cranium: thick, solid, hard, yellow bone without a visible medullary portion
  • Extramedullary hematopoietic activity enlarges the central core, leaving only a thin rim of cortical bone
  • All bones, including phalanges, show a reticular pattern indicating hematopoiesis
    • Long bones, more so the phalanges, normally do not contribute much
Clinical cue Severe anemia recruits all bones to active duty.

"Chipmunk facies"

  • Facial abnormality from hyperactivity and overexpression of the maxilla
  • Enlarged cheek bone pulls on the nasal bridge, causing it to flatten
  • Malar prominence
  • Flattening and widening of nasal bridge
  • Exposure of upper central teeth
  • Frontal bossing

Laboratory Diagnosis p. 13

Hb electrophoresis

  • Definitive diagnosis based on identification of abnormal Hb
  • β-Thalassemia: β-globin is absent → α-globin combines with other globins → α2δ2 (HbA2) or α2γ2 (HbF)
  • α-Thalassemia: α-globin is absent → 4 β-globin (HbH) or 4 γ-globin (Barts Hb)
Table 8. Hb electrophoresis findings in thalassemia
Thalassemia typeLaboratory findings
β-Thalassemia MajorMarked elevation of HbA2 (α2δ2) or HbF (α2γ2), no HbA
β-Thalassemia MinorSlightly INC (4–8%) HbA2 (α2δ2) or HbF (α2γ2), DEC HbA
α-ThalassemiaHbH (4β) in adults or Barts Hb (4γ) in infants

Peripheral blood smear

  • Hypochromic, microcytic anemia
    • Any abnormality of Hb will cause hypochromic, microcytic anemia
  • With target cells: produced when abnormal Hb collects in the center of RBC
  • With basophilic stippling: due to the inclusion of aggregated abnormal chains
Table 9. Hypochromic microcytic anemia Must Know
IDAThalassemiaChronic disease
Serum Fe↓↑↓
Serum Ferritin↓↑↑
TIBC↑↓↓
% Saturation↓↑↑
MorphologyH/MH/MN/N or H/M
RDW↑↑N/↑N

H/M = hypochromic/microcytic · N/N = normochromic/normocytic

Lecturer emphasis · Iron transport
  • TIBC and % saturation measure the transport form of iron
  • Think of a bus containing iron: % saturation = seats in the bus that contain iron
  • TIBC = seats that do not contain iron

Evidence of bone marrow hyperplasia

  • Chronic hemolysis → EJK
    • Erythroid hyperplasia: INC reticulocyte count and presence of normoblasts (normally only in the bone marrow)
    • Chromatosis: due to iron overload

Iron overload

  • Marked INC in siderocytes, sideroblasts in bone marrow, and hemochromatosis
    • Siderocytes & sideroblasts: blast cells containing much iron
    • Hemochromatosis from shortened life span of abnormal RBCs and transfused RBCs
  • Biggest problem in thalassemia
  • Cause of death: severe deposition of iron and hemosiderin in the heart (cardiac hemochromatosis) → heart failure
Lecturer emphasis · Ineffective erythropoiesis
  • BM produces red cells with defective globin
  • Releases iron into serum, causing elevation of iron in thalassemia
  • Amount of hemolysis is more than what sweat can release → INC iron in the body

E. Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH) p. 13–14

  • Causes paroxysmal chronic intravascular hemolysis
  • One of the few hemoglobinopathies that produce intravascular rather than extravascular hemolysis

Pathology

Inactivation or loss of PIGA gene (phosphatidylinositol glycan group A)
Deficient production of stem cell proteins CD59, CD55, C8 protein
Susceptibility to lysis by complement
  • These stem cell proteins are inhibitors of complement-mediated lysis of RBCs
    • CD59: lysis inhibitor
    • CD55: decay accelerating factor
    • C8 protein: for binding
  • In their absence, lysis easily occurs, particularly in an acidic environment (i.e., during sleep)
  • Also affects platelets and WBCs (from hematopoietic stem cells)
    • INC episodes of venous thrombosis due to platelet defects (usual cause of death)
    • INC risk of acute myeloid leukemia due to WBC stem cell defects

Signs and symptoms

  • Reddish urine upon waking
  • Intravascular hemolysis → mild hemoglobinuria, iron deficiency anemia
  • Hemolysis is nocturnal in only 25% of cases
  • Symptoms are usually mild, but workup should be done due to the complications involved

F. Immunohemolytic Anemia (IHA) / Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (AHA) p. 14

  • Hemolysis due to appearance of antibodies that attack the body's own RBCs
  • Major diagnostic criterion: Coomb's antiglobulin test
  • Classified into warm antibody IHA, cold agglutinin IHA, and cold hemolysin IHA
Warm antibody IHACold agglutinin IHACold hemolysin IHA
AntibodyIgGIgMIgG
Active tempBody temperature (37˚C)
  • Binds at 0–4˚C
  • Complement activation at slightly higher temp
  • Dissociates at 30˚C
  • Binds RBC and complement at low temperature/cold areas
  • Hemolysis starts as temperature rises (recirculates to warm parts)
ComplementDoes not fix complementActivates complementFixes complement
Hemolysis
  • Extravascular, rupture in the spleen → splenomegaly
  • IgG-coated RBC binds monocytes and splenic macrophages
IntravascularMassive intravascular
Causes
  • Mostly idiopathic
  • Drugs, tumors (lymphoma, leukemia/neoplasia), autoimmune disorders (e.g. SLE)
Infection: mycoplasma pneumonia and infectious mononucleosisInfections: mycoplasma pneumonia, measles, mumps, other viral flu-like syndromes
WarmingKeeping the patient warm prevents agglutination and/or improves symptomsWarming aggravates the condition rather than alleviates it
Other nameParoxysmal cold hemoglobinuria
Key differentiator
  • Those that fix complement cause intravascular hemolysis
  • Warm antibody IHA does not, so it is extravascular
  • Cold hemolysin is more serious than cold agglutinin: massive intravascular hemolysis after cold exposure that is not improved by keeping the patient warm
Mnemonics (stated in the lecture)
  • "Warm weather is Great for Swimming" → Warm antibody IHA produces IgG active at 37˚C leading to Splenomegaly
  • "Cold weather is Mmmm so stay Indoors" → Cold agglutinin IHA produces IgM active at 0–4˚C leading to Intravascular hemolysis

Cold agglutinin: clinical considerations

  • Theoretically, at body temperature (37˚C) the antibody should not cause problems (active at 0–4˚C, inactive at 30˚C)
  • Situations that cause antibody activation and intravascular hemolysis:
    • Transfusion of blood that has not been warmed: blood bank refrigerated blood must be warmed prior to transfusion so antibodies dissociate and inactivate
    • Significantly DEC temperature in superficial vessels (e.g., ears, fingers) in snow countries with freezing temperatures

G. Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia p. 14

  • Results from trauma to RBCs as they negotiate narrow obstruction in the microvasculature
    • Obstruction affects small rather than medium-sized or large vessels
    • DIC, TTP, SLE, or malignant hypertension produce microthrombi obstructing small vessels
    • Results in RBC fragmentation through narrow areas
  • PBS: RBCs with variable shapes and loss of segments called schistocytes
  • Same trauma when RBCs pass through prosthetic valves or burned areas of the body

Case Pearls from the Formative Quiz Rationales p. 15–18

Lecture-specific note
  • These are the teaching points stated in the trans's quiz rationales
  • The questions themselves are not reproduced

Reading a hypochromic microcytic case

  • MCV ↓ and MCHC ↓ = hypochromic microcytic (e.g., MCV 77 fL, MCHC 29)
  • Smear: RBCs smaller than normal with a large central pallor
    • Normally, RBC diameter is about the same size as the nucleus of the smallest lymphocyte
Distinguishing hypochromic microcytic causes (quiz rationale)
AnemiaTeaching points
Iron deficiency anemia
  • Nutritional anemia (lack of iron, B12, or folic acid): retic count not expected to elevate until treatment is given
  • No history of previous hospitalization favors IDA
  • Give iron
Thalassemia
  • A form of hemolysis → retic count increased (marrow compensates)
  • Most have previous hospitalizations due to transfusions
  • Withhold iron: iron deposits in the heart (cardiac failure) and pancreas (brown diabetes)
Anemia of chronic disease
  • WBC expected to be elevated due to inflammation
  • Circulating iron is low, but storage and transport form is high (hard to transfer iron to blood when sick)
  • Hepcidin (inflammatory mediator) elevated → DEC iron absorption → DEC serum iron
  • Don't give iron
  • Treat the disease first
Anemia of renal diseaseNormochromic, normocytic

Megaloblastic anemia (B12 or folate deficiency)

  • Chronic diarrhea may cause poor absorption → deficiency
  • MCV high, MCHC high
LabFinding
Peripheral smear
  • Macrocytic "hyperchromic" RBC, presence of megaloblasts
  • Leukopenia with hypersegmented neutrophils or "macropolys" (normal neutrophil has 3–4 lobes)
  • Decreased platelets
RBC indicesIncreased MCV, high normal MCHC
Retic count
  • Decreased or normal until treatment
  • Striking reticulocytosis at least 5 days after treatment
Bone marrow
  • Hyperplasia upon treatment
  • N:C asynchronism: cytoplasm matures while the nucleus does not (lack of B12)
Metabolites
  • Methylmalonic acid increases in absence of B12 → neurologic abnormalities
  • Homocysteine increases in folic acid and B12 deficiency

Reddish urine after antimalarial drugs (G6PD)

  • Reddish urine: red blood cells → glomerulonephritis vs hemoglobin → hemoglobinuria (more tea colored)
  • Normocytic normochromic anemia with bite cells, jaundice (hemolysis), negative splenomegaly
  • Sickle cell may look like bite cells, but hypoxia triggers sickle cell while drug intake triggers G6PD
  • Spherocytosis: no triggering factors, extravascular
  • PNH: no triggering factors, but the only other intravascular condition aside from G6PD
Choosing the test
TestUse
Hb electrophoresisDetects abnormal hemoglobin: thalassemia (HbA2, HbF) and sickle cell (HbS)
Coombs testAutoimmune hemolytic anemia: antibodies on the surface of red cells
Osmotic fragility testHereditary spherocytosis: spherical cells easily lyse in water
Bone marrow biopsyDone in the presence of malignancy

Aplastic anemia

  • Bone marrow is mostly composed of fat cells compared to hematopoietic elements
  • 1 is to 1 or 50% is the normal composition for adults
  • WBC & platelets are expected to be low

Bleeding Disorders (from quiz rationales)

HemophiliaVon Willebrand disorderITPTTP
Platelet countNormalLow (thrombocytopenia)Consumption of platelets
Bleeding time (BT)NormalElevatedIncreased (reflects ↓ platelet number)
Clotting time (CT)ElevatedElevatedNormal (clotting factors intact)
PT / aPTT
  • PT normal (extrinsic normal)
  • aPTT elevated (intrinsic problem)
aPTT elevated
Key pointMost common intrinsic pathway abnormality: Factor VIII
  • vWF stabilizes factor VIII, prolonging its half-life
  • Without vWF, factor VIII ↓ → prolonged aPTT
Trauma-related ecchymosis, petechiae, menorrhagia with normal WBC and RBC
  • Systemic disease such as fever
  • Microthrombi
  • ADAMTS13 deficiency (cleaves vWF)
  • Can cause neurologic symptoms

Cram Sheet

Red exclamation points (lecture wording)
  • Non-functioning marrow: DEC reticulocyte count in anemia indicates bone marrow failure
  • MCV and MCHC are best used in determining RBC morphology
  • EJK: Erythroid hyperplasia, Jaundice, Chromatosis/Color
  • Methemoglobinemia: from oxidation of hemoglobin to methemoglobin
  • DEC serum haptoglobin: important laboratory parameter in the diagnosis of intravascular hemolysis
  • Jaundice, anemia: common to both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis
  • Majority of hemolysis from an intrinsic red cell defect occurs in the spleen or is extravascular
  • Splenomegaly does not occur in IVH since the spleen is the site of lysis for the defective RBCs
  • INC in reticulocytes is expected in hemolytic anemia
  • G6PD: two types of hemolysis present
  • Vaso-occlusive crisis: multiple, simultaneous painful thrombosis in different organs
  • Subtypes of β-thalassemia and α-thalassemia (Tables 6, 7), and the hypochromic microcytic anemia table (Table 9)

Core definitions

  • Anemia: reduction of the total circulating red cell mass to below normal limits → DEC oxygen transport
  • Hemolytic anemia: INC destruction of red cells → survival <120 days
  • HSC: pluripotent or multipotent cell capable of self renewal
  • Reticulocyte: young RBC that lost its nucleus
    • First cell in the peripheral blood
  • Autosplenectomy: repeated infarction, repair, fibrosis → completely fibrotic spleen
  • Schistocytes: RBCs with variable shapes and loss of segments (microangiopathic)

G6PD deficiency

Oxidant (drugs, fava, infection, stress)
No NADPH, reduced glutathione → NADP, H2O2, Hb+3 (ROS)
H2O2 → intravascular (predominant)
Hb+3 → Heinz bodies → spleen plucks → bite cells (mild extravascular)

Sickle cell

Deoxygenation
HbS polymerizes → sickling
(1) chronic extravascular hemolysis · (2) small vessel occlusion → pain

PNH

PIGA loss
↓ CD59 (lysis inhibitor), CD55 (DAF), C8 (binding)
Complement lysis in acidic sleep → reddish morning urine · venous thrombosis (death) · AML risk

Common exam traps
  • Oliguria appears only if anemia is due to blood loss, not hemoglobinopathy or nutritional anemia
  • Koilonychia is not specific for anemia (also chronic lung disease)
  • HbA1C is not involved in hematologic disorders
  • In G6PD, intravascular outweighs extravascular even though bite cells are splenic
  • Sickle cell symptoms never appear before 6 months (HbF protects)
  • Sickle cell anemia has DEC osmotic fragility
  • HS hemolyzes earlier (higher concentration)
  • Cold hemolysin worsens with warming
  • Cold agglutinin improves with warming
  • Warm IHA is extravascular (no complement fixation)
  • Thalassemia: serum Fe and ferritin ↑ and withhold iron
  • ACD: ferritin ↑ but serum Fe ↓
  • α-thalassemia is less severe than β because β and γ chains are more soluble

Warnings / causes of death

  • Thalassemia: iron overload is the biggest problem → cardiac hemochromatosis → heart failure
  • PNH: venous thrombosis is the usual cause of death
  • Sickle cell anemia: fatal at 20 y/o
    • Pulmonary infection → fatal cycle of hypoxia, sickling, vasoocclusion
  • Cold agglutinin: warm stored blood before transfusion
  • Sickle cell: avoid dehydration, acidosis, infection, stasis
